titleStmt.title: Interview with Opal Land Nelson, Undated
titleStmt.author: Gary Rhay and Alison McGann [transcriber]

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Opal Land Nelson was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Start by having you give us your name, and spell your last name for us again.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Okay. My name is Opal Nelson, and N-e-l-s-o-n.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Now, Opal, if you -- where were when the war broke out?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: I was back in Indiana just two years out of high school, and in Huntington actually, working at a small coil factory which actually was, I think, making coils for the war effort, because that was about a year before I left. With the war -- with the war starting in December of '41, then I left home in January of '43 to go out to California.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Tell me, first of all, how did you hear about Pearl Harbor and the attack there, and how did that change life in Huntington for you guys right there --

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Oh --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: -- that first little bit?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Totally. We heard it over the radio, of course. There was no TV. And it was really hard to comprehend the scope of what it would eventually become. But it was -- it was pretty -- it was frightening because I had three brothers, lot of cousins, male cousins, and so forth. And it was pretty frightening because -- partly because of the uncertainty, you know, what was going to happen and what would happen.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Let me have your glasses.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: You're clicking your glasses.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Uh oh.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: That's okay. Pretty normal reaction.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Click, click.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: You know, if we let people sit in a chair that moves, whether they want to or not, they just automatically move, so...

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay, so after you get over it -- well, let's talk about President Roosevelt's speech. I'm sure you listened to that. How did you feel after -- during that speech and after that speech. Did it reassure you, or...

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, of course, we all gathered around the radio to listen, holding our breath, and it didn't really -- it didn't really make us feel any better. In fact, it kind of made it a little more scary because we still didn't know what was happening, or what would happen. But we knew it was monumental and would be quite a reference, or quite an impact on history. Of course, that doesn't -- that doesn't hit you yet. You're still, you know, you're still in shock wondering what's going to happen.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Could you take a minute and talk about how the -- how you think the country felt about President Roosevelt and having him as the President. Did that make a difference for the country?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, everybody was just very confident with President Roosevelt, mainly because those of us who were of any age can remember him bringing us out of the Depression and the different programs that he started: the WPA, the CCC, Civilian Conservation Corps. And starting all those programs that was bringing everybody out of the -- out of the Depression, and everybody was very, very confident and trusting in his judgment. I remember when he was starting to run for a third term and there were billboards up around the country, and it showed Uncle Sam with his thumbs down, and it says "no third term." But everybody was comfortable with the third term because of what he had done for the country, starting the Social Security and starting these programs to get -- to get the people back into the workforce and give the young people something to do. And it was -- everybody was very confident.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Now let's talk about life in Huntington and how that changed in the first months of the war: rationing, victory drives, and war bonds, and things like that.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: There was a lot of that. Some of it didn't make much sense to me. I was -- what was I? About 19. Saving old tires, saving aluminum, you know, picking the tin cans, and so forth. I couldn't see whether that was -- where that was a help for the war effort. But in the rationing, I could see where that would help. And, of course, we all had the ration books, and we didn't plan on buying shoes, we couldn't buy gas -- only so much according to the ticket, and so forth. That's one way it changed. The other way it changed was because here was all my contemporary friends going off to war, which was pretty scary having never lived through a war before. And my classmates in school, neighbors, everybody was going, many -- good percentage of them that actually volunteered, you know, didn't wait for the draft. So, there was a big exodus of my friends going off to war.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, how did you come to the decision to leave Huntington and go somewhere else? How did that come about?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, I guess I always had a kind of a wanderlust. I had made a couple of trips before, one down into Texas to drive a migrant family home because their oldest son, the only driver, had been drafted, and I volunteered to take them back. We were acquainted, you know, it wasn't just somebody out of the blue. And then I had -- I had gone to St. Louis for a couple of months, I guess, just for an adventure. I don't know why. But it was -- so when my girlfriend and I got to talking one night, and we decided we'd like to get into the war effort, and the place to be would be California where the aircraft plants were. And so we made the decision to go from Huntington out to California. And it shows how we were so -- we planned ahead so well, because we only had enough money to get to Denver Colorado. And we went that far, got a job in a restaurant and worked about six weeks, and got enough money to go on out to California. So when we got to California, it was -- I remember it was just a beautiful day, clear, warm, and we had come from Indiana, or Denver actually, in January. But anyway, so we -- we went the first day we got there. We went up to the Douglas aircraft plant, and all they did was just give us a very basic physical, told us to be at work the next day. It was just immediate.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: How did you find out about the Douglas plant?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: I think through the newspaper. The first day we got to California we looked in a newspaper and found out they were hiring. So -- and we didn't know what jobs we were going to end up with until we got there the next day. So...

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Tell us about the next --

sp.speaker: Unidentified person
sp.p: I'm sorry, can you move a little to your left please?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So, tell us about the next day what --

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Oh we were --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: -- what was that like, the indoctrination?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Yeah. We were so excited. We got up there and they -- they didn't ask us, they just placed us. And I -- they placed me in what they called the floor, and -- as a riveter. What happened was, we were working on the A20 Havoc, and they would -- the two sides of the fuselage would come down the line on a jig. And they would do all the riveting there and put the skin on and rivet, well, rivet the frame together first and then put the skin on. And then it got down to the end of the line, they would take the two halves of the fuselage off the jigs and put it on what they called the floor. And there, we would pick up the rivets that they could not reach while it was on the jig. So it wasn't just straight do this, do that, this line, that line. It was to pick up the little, little places that they couldn't reach when it was on the jig. And they gave me a man partner. And most of the men that had worked there had gone through aircraft school, maybe just a few months. I don't know how long. And so here came these teenyboppers that not only were young but they were women. And they weren't too happy about that. But my partner, I decided that I was going to like him even though he didn't like me. And when we -- when we were doing the actual job, he was on the outside of the fuselage, and I was on the inside, so we couldn't see each other. And so I -- I'd always been fairly handy with tools and kind of an outdoors person, so it was easy for me to get the idea of the bucking bar and which side to use and where to use it, and so forth. So...

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, tell us a little bit about exactly what you wound up doing then. Let's -- let's talk about what you'd actually do to fix a rivet. I mean everybody knows what a "Rosie the Riveter" is, but talk us through what you remember about actually putting a rivet in the skin.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Yeah. We had to learn the different sizes of rivets, or the different types, either flush, or round head, or whatever. And the riveting gun -- of course you had a long hose -- and the riveting gun wasn't heavy. I mean, my dad worked on the railroad and he put rivets in bridges, so I expected the rivets to be three inches long and weigh a half a pound, you know. But here's these little teeny, tiny ones that went in the skin of the airplane. And so my partner would put the rivet in from the outside, and he'd hit it once. If you'd just pull one little thing, it'll hit it once, and I was supposed to be on the other end with a bucking bar. And so we kind of got a rhythm arranged and learned, I guess, where we -- he would hit the rivet, and I would be on it. And we'd just go right down the line of where we were putting the rivets in. And then there were some where I not only had the rivet gun but I also had the bucking bar. And I would -- like, there were the lightening holes they called it, along the edge up at the top of the fuselage, and I would do both. I would be riveting, but I would be holding the bucking bar on the outside -- I mean on the inside -- and do the riveting all by myself. And it was fun. It was fun. I enjoyed it. Sometimes I would think about, you know, where it was going and what we were doing, but most -- most of the time we were just so busy trying to get it done -- get the job done that we didn't have many projected thoughts of where they were going.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: When you did think about that, what kind of thoughts did you have?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, it was mostly in the evening. I worked graveyard all the time. And it was mostly when we would go out at 10:30 at night to catch the bus to go to -- go to work. And you'd see these searchlights zeroing in on a little airplane going along, maybe quite a ways up. Or you'd hear -- you'd hear some, I don't know, I guess they were not gunshots but some kind of noise. It sounded like gunshots. And I don't know whether they were -- I know they weren't shooting at an airplane. Maybe they were practicing or something. But we had right in back of where our apartment was, they had set up a little -- it was an army camp because there was several, I don't know, several troops back there. And they were one of them that had a searchlight, and their job was to keep surveilling the skies to see where the airplanes were. And when I'd -- when we would come out to go to work and see these searchlights going around it, it was pretty scary. And then it would kind of hit us what we were doing.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well how about your partner, did he ever warm up to you?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Slightly. [Laughter.] It was just very slightly, but he did get to be fairly civil during the time I worked with him.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Do you think that the women in general at the aircraft plant were treated fairly, or...

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Yes. With a few exceptions, a few exceptions. Most of them -- most of the men were very considerate and may be a little overly so because we were women. But a lot of them just kind of -- they didn't ignore us, but they just kind of took us for granted. And we were there, and they didn't have any control over us being there, and so they just kind of accepted us, I guess.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Fair enough.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Do you remember what your wages were? Was it pretty good? Or...

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, it was very good for what we had been -- what we had been making because it was -- I can't think exactly. Seems to me it was like 43 cents an hour. And then later it was a little more. But we worked -- we worked just five days a week. We didn't work much overtime. And I can't remember, it seems like it added up to somewhere around $50. Was that a week or every two weeks? I don't know. I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, where were you guys staying?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: We had an apartment in a little house that they had taken and made three apartments in: one upstairs; ours was in the back; there was one apartment in the front. And it was very, very small. But so many of the people did that with their houses. They -- they'd make apartments and just barely enough room, you know. We did have a bedroom, a very small living room, and a very small kitchen, so -- and our own entrance, of course. So many people even took garages and made an apartment out of them, kind of like a studio apartment. But ours was in a small house on Ocean Avenue, and it was in a -- kind of in an area where there was a lot of apartment buildings. And I've been back since then and, of course, those apartment buildings have been torn down and they put the high-rises there, right where our house was. So I kind of watched it through the years develop into one of the -- where they have the big hotels and apartments.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Now you mentioned that you took the bus to work. Was that provided by the company or was that a city bus, or...

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: No, it was just a city bus. And it -- I think it made a run, like, every ten minutes or so and would drop us off right at the door of Douglas. The factory itself, I don't really know how big it was, but it was totally covered with camouflage. And there was no way that we could see what it looked like, but I had been told looked like the Ocean Park Avenue came up, and from the sky it looked like it just continued on. But underneath all the camouflage was Douglas Aircraft.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What other kind of security measures did you see at the factory? Did you see guards and checkpoints and things like that?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, not to -- not to a great degree. But we did have to wear our badges, and without the badge we couldn't get in the door. They did kind of watch for cameras, and there was a security guard right by the door as we went in. But they -- other than checking the badge, I don't think they did any checking. And of course, we had to check in with a time clock and check out with a time clock. But other than that, there wasn't any security. There was a lady matron who made the rounds of the restrooms all the time to be sure somebody wasn't sleeping the night away. But, I think other than that, I -- we didn't feel like we were being watched. We were just kind of being trusted, you know.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: How about in the surrounding area? You mentioned the searchlights and things like that. What other defensive things did you see while you were there in California? What other things were going on that looked like they were trying to defend the United States?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, we were only about a block and a half from the beach, and we would walk up and down the beach. There were several bunkers up -- we could see up on the hills. And I don't know whether, how many people were manning them, but they were just small. But they were like a concrete bunker. And I don't know what kind of ammunition and things they had up there, but there were several of those along as we walked down the beach, we could see them up there. And then the unit that was in back of our apartment took up about a city block, and you could hear them marching to cadence, and so forth. But we didn't have a car. We were -- we were just bus people. And so we had -- we had freedom. But the bunkers and searchlights, and so forth, all that was -- it was there. And we were aware of them. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Did they -- were they still doing the blackout and things like that?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Oh yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Talk to us a little about blackout.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Total blackout. It was amazing because -- it wasn't very long til I had a boyfriend, of course. And he had a little -- I think it was a little 1940 Crosley car. And you had to tape -- put black tape over the front -- the top half of the headlights. And then you could only drive with parking lights on. And so it was pretty hard to see where you were going. But no outside lights, no supposed, you know, matches to light a cigarette or whatever. That was pretty strict. And if you did have any kind of a light, then it had to be sheltered from the sky so that it couldn't be seen from the air.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, since you worked night shift, the graveyard shift, at the factory, what kind of things did they do there to keep the lights from showing.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, the lights, like the door that you entered in, it was -- it had a shield over the top or kind of a roof-like thing. Very dim light. But after you got inside, then everything was very brightly lit and with fluorescent lights and so forth. But I don't know. I don't think the camouflage over the top -- I don't think that kept the lights from showing through because it was just kind of like netting with paint show -- making it look like bushes and streets and so forth, houses.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Let's see here. I had this great question and suddenly lost it. Just one of those things.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: [Laughter.] I have the same problem.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, it's okay. So is there anything else about the work at Douglas that you want to talk about.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, I -- we had a really nice boss. His last name was Duncan. You know, everybody called everybody by their last name. I don't know why. But I have no idea what his first name was, but his last name was Duncan, and he was very, very good to -- to us lady workers, especially if there was a little problem with the men having so many women. But he was really good. And, and let's see, I had another thought, too. And the fellow I worked with was -- his name was Miller, and like I said, he did get to where he was a little more friendly and more accepting. And there happened to be another fellow working there by the name of Nelson. And he was the one I eventually married. So we met there. But one thing I did was, they told us at the plant -- I don't know whether they handed out a brochure or what, but they were needing Red Cross nurse aids in the hospitals because so many of the nurses had left to go to war. And so I would come home at 7:00 in the morning, go to a 9:00 o'clock class for nurse aid, and that went on for about six weeks, and I got my certificate. And then usually in the evening, like between 6:00 and 10:00, I'd volunteer at the hospitals to help with the nurse aid chores and taking care of the patients, and so forth. And I really liked that. I enjoyed that. One problem we did have between our social life and our business life, and whatever, we had a hard time finding time to sleep. [Laughter.] So we had to -- usually on weekends, we had to take time to catch up on our sleep.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: We need to change -- [Interruption in video feed.]

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Interesting that your dad had a -- had a show there --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Yeah, it's fun.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So, you -- you kind of talked around the problems. Were there other problems with the men besides they just kind of ignored you and...

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: No. I've heard that there were problems with the other men, but I -- the area where I was working, they were just really friendly. In fact, one of them ended up being the best man at our wedding. It just seemed like we were all friends and everybody looking out for each other. And we used to get out off work at 7:00 in the morning and do things together like going ice skating or horseback riding. We'd go out to one of the ranches there, and went -- used to go up -- -- they had a -- what they called a B19 club. And it was up in the Santa Monica hills there somewhere, I don't know where. And we'd go up there for breakfast, the whole group of us, and so it did -- it did seem more like a -- almost a family group. So, no, I didn't have any -- any trouble with the --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Now was your husband in your area somewhere or did you meet him --

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Yes. Actually he was in working the same department, and I first found out he was interested in me by throwing clecos at me. If you'd know what a cleco is, it's a little device that you -- spring device -- that you put -- you put on a -- through the skin to hold it while you rivet up to there. And then you take the cleco out and put the last rivet in. And they're just little spring devices about that big. And then he asked me out, and we went to what they call the "People Are Funny" radio show. And I eventually ended up on it. And it was -- it was before Art Linkletter had the show. I don't remember the name of the people, but anyway, my project was that I was to ride the roller coaster at Ocean Park, and while I was riding the roller coaster, I was supposed to be reciting the names of states. And I was going to be paid according to the number of states that I could name while I was going on this roller coaster. [Laughter.] And I think I got about six. You can't think very good on a roller coaster. But people all over the country, relatives, happened to hear that program and hear me on it. So that was just some of things we did in the evening.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, I'm glad you brought up your husband and everything because the obvious question is, you know, you had -- what did you do when you weren't working? You talked about volunteering at the hospital, and maybe you'd like to talk about that a little more and the rest of the social-life kind of things that you had there.

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, working in the hospital was really fun. I enjoyed it. And at first they had me going around filling water jugs and so forth. I didn't care for that. But then eventually they let me help take care of the patients. And like, we learned to give a bed bath, and to help people take their first steps after surgery, and, and that type of thing. We had a definite uniform. It was a white blouse with a Red Cross emblem on the shoulder and a -- kind of a blue denim pinafore, which I thought I had lost it, but I finally found it in a box in the attic. And so I still have my uniform. Doesn't fit anymore, but I still have it. But --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Too big right?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Pardon me?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: It's too big now?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Yes, it's way too big -- to go around my neck. [Laugher.] But a lot of the people that were in the hospital were -- had been working at Douglas. Maybe they'd got their -- got injured some way or other, finger in the punch press, or something. And so it was interesting talking to the people that I took care of. And so, it was also a very gratifying thing. I just really felt good about doing that. And of course, like I say, it was all volunteer. But it also gave me an interest in nursing that I eventually went to nurses training. I didn't quite get through, but -- but as a result of that.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What other kinds of social things did you do while you were there?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: We did a lot of going to the beach. In fact, sometimes we'd get off work at 7:00 in the morning, take a towel or a blanket, and go down to the beach and sleep. Which was kind of a mistake because fair-skin people have done that and got pretty burnt. But -- and I did get a few sunburns, but I tanned easy. So, mostly, it was getting together with other people we were working with and doing things like that. There was a lot of servicemen on the street. They were -- all kinds, either on leave or on their way to somewhere. And very often down on the beach we would see a whole -- I don't know what -- company or something doing their calisthenics out on the sand. So it was just kind of everywhere you looked, there were servicemen. And at that time, the servicemen didn't even have to hold up their thumb. Anybody that would see a serviceman beside their street, or like they were headed somewhere, people would stop and pick them up. It was just kind of like they felt it was their -- something they wanted to do. But as far as we were -- as far as social life, we were pretty busy just with our daily routine.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What about the -- talk for a minute about the motivation. What caused you to want to be involved in this? Was it wanting to be away from home, or wanting to earn money, or just be a part of what was going on? Or a combination of that?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, it was kind of a combination of the excitement of being off on our own, and, and the money, I think, was basically the beginning motivation. But after we got out there and got to work, got to realize what we were doing, it was more a feeling of doing something rather than just sitting and waiting. And we really felt like that we were actually doing something for the war effort.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Now looking back, what do you think the contribution of the women was during the war?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Oh, I think it was tremendous. In fact, everybody my age that I talk to, just, with very few exceptions, had some kind of a job. I discovered a couple of women I've known for years, and one was a welder in Long Beach during the war. The other one was working in a munitions plant where they were making -- actually making the bullets. And these are things I didn't even realize. I just -- after we got to talking about the Rosie the Riveter Association, I found all kinds of my friends had worked there. And I think -- I think the women made a tremendous impact because a lot of us were just out of high school, maybe never had a job away from home, and it was just opening up a whole new territory for women. Before that, it was either menial jobs or it was -- unless you had a college education, which most people didn't in those days because, couldn't afford it, there wasn't the money. And it just opened up a whole new spectrum for women.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: How about the idea of (rural) farm girls from Huntington, Indiana, that show up in cosmopolitan California? Did that open your eyes to a bigger world and to different kinds of people and things?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, it did. Not to the degree that it would have today, I'm sure, because we were pretty naive, even though I was almost 21. That would be like about a 14-year-old now. But we were -- we were all family raised, we were raised in the church, and we -- we just didn't ever think about getting in trouble. We didn't drink, we didn't smoke, we didn't -- of course there wasn't any drugs then. And if somebody was just a little bit on the wild side, why, we left them alone. And we just kind of did our thing, and did what was required of us, and what we did to have fun. And looking back it's amazing, as naive as we were, that we didn't get into some kind of trouble. But we didn't. My girlfriend eventually went back to Indiana and married a guy back there. And then, and then I married my husband Jim on the 29th of February, 1944. And mainly because he was a lead man at that time, and he had been getting deferments because he was working on the A20. Well, along about -- let's see, we were married in February, and we decided to go ahead and get married because he was getting one deferment after the other because of being a lead man. So we married in February, and by September they -- they cancelled the contract on the A20. And so there was about two weeks in between when Jim got his notice from the draft board. And he was drafted then in October of that year and was gone to the South Pacific for two years. And so that was the two years I went back to Indiana, for those two years. And that was kind of interesting, too, or it is for me. I hadn't been back there maybe a year -- maybe a month, and there was an ad in the paper that they needed a trained porter, they called it. And what it was is they wanted to hire a woman who would go on the train and ride over to Marion, Ohio, clean the restrooms, clean the cars. They were just totally loaded. I mean it was really hard to get a seat on a train. And there'd been families with little children, and so forth. And my job would be to just kind of be a stewardess, I guess you call it. And so I worked at that the two years that I was home. And that was real interesting because I was very talkative, obviously, and I talked to the servicemen coming home and the families that were going somewhere to meet the serviceman and so forth. And it was very interesting -- very. Bedsides being a job.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, since -- well, how about war news? How did you guys, both in California and when you got back to Indiana, how did you hear about what was going on in the war?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Mostly through the newspapers. And while I was home and Jim was overseas, it was the radio. Of course we had a radio, and we'd sit around every night and listen to the war news. Also the Movietone news in the theaters would have a lot of war news going. And that was just about what we heard or how we heard.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Ever see an A20 in a Movietone clip and say, hey, that's what I used to do?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: No. I never did, but I have a little lapel pin that's an A20, and twice, within the last few years, I've had, surprisingly, a young man see that say, "That's an A20." I said, "How did you know that? You weren't even born." And they -- they either studied aviation, or studied the war or something, and they recognized the lapel pin I had on. That was -- was strange.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Since you had a husband in the military, how important was mail, and what was that like?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Oh, very important. I know we used to write back and forth almost every day, and there was a time there when it went about two and a half weeks, and I didn't get any mail. And when I did, I got about, oh, maybe 12, 13 letters, but they were muddy. They were, oh, they -- I should have kept them, but I didn't. And so when I finally did realize, or get the letters, he was on the invasion of Okinawa. And he was on there for 54 days. And he said out of 54 days, it probably rained 53 and a half. I think that's exaggerated, but there was a lot of mud. And that explained the mud on the letters. It really scared me when I saw them, but he said that's the way it was. It was mud all over.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Did they censor his letters coming back to you?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah, especially the V-mail. He sent quite a few V-mail, and there'd be pieces of it cut out. I don't know, they didn't have felt pens in those days, I guess, because there'd be pieces of it cut out, especially if he would say something like "next week we will be going to" and that would be cut out. Or if he'd say, "we just came from whatever" and that would be cut out.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Tell us what V-mail was?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: V-mail was -- you had to take a certain piece of paper that was made for that, write your letter like 8 1/2 by 11, and you write your letter on that, and they would photograph it and put it on film, and send the film with I don't know how many thousands of letters on it. And then, I don't know where, I assume in the States, that they would then print the letters off. But when you got the letter it was about maybe 4 by 6. It was very small, so sometimes you had to get a magnifying glass to read it. But it was very efficient, very efficient, and they would -- I got quite a few V-mail letters. And it's -- it was quick. I think it was quicker than the regular mail. It seemed like it anyway. It'd just be a matter of two or three days that I'd get a V-mail, but a regular mail would take probably a week.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Do you recall when President Roosevelt died?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Just vaguely. I -- I don't remember. I don't remember where I was or what -- what was happening at that time.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. How about when the war ended? How did you feel about that?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Oh, boy. That was a real celebration. V-J day especially, because I was still back at my home in Indiana, and my sisters and I went to town. We lived about six miles out of town. We went to town and the streets were just jammed. People and -- people on radiators, and on the tops of cars, and they were just driving up and down the main street and back and forth, and there was a lot of yelling and shouting and singing, and everybody was celebrating.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Do you remember hearing about the atomic bomb and have any thoughts about that?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, yes, and, and this is -- this is kind of -- I don't know, but I need to mention this. My mother was raised a Quaker and she was very, very peace-minded. And she used to have a peace team from the Quaker church would come, and they'd have meetings in our house. And, and so I've always had that pull of the peace that I was raised up in and the war effort, and it was -- it was kind of a pull. And I -- I rationalized that what I was doing for the war effort was helping to bring peace. And so it was, it was kind of -- you ask about the atomic bomb. I really -- it was really scary for me because -- and for a lot of people I'm sure -- because they didn't know what the eventual effect would be or how far it would go. And so, well, I suppose the authorities knew, but the ordinary layperson did not know. So it was -- it was pretty scary. But it brought peace. And I know my husband was on -- after they secured Okinawa, he was headed for the Sea of Japan. So they were -- they were planning an invasion of Japan right after that. But because they dropped the bomb and the war ended, then they didn't go ahead with the invasion of Japan, of course.

sp.speaker: Unidentified person
sp.p: (?Got another?) three or four minutes.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Did I leave anything out?

sp.speaker: Unidentified person
sp.p: I can't think of anything.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Unidentified person
sp.p: Posterity and --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Yeah. Is there anything you just want to add for posterity's sake to this tape?

sp.speaker: Opal Land Nelson
sp.p: Well, just that it was an amazing experience, but at the time, we didn't realize that it was. And I -- I would say that many, many times through my life that the experience of not only being on their -- on our own, and also the experience of helping with the war effort, has come back to me several times -- well, many times, in a -- in a positive way. And almost like whatever it is that comes up, we can do it. We can handle it. And that's -- that was a good -- a good effect, I think. I don't know whether it was the confidence we got in doing that, or in being on our own, or what, but it just gave us a feeling of confidence that whatever came up, we can handle it.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Great.
